front: Hudson: what does it mean if you are scared to feel an emotion?
back: You are already in that emotion. The fear is the feeling arriving.
source_title: 50 lessons on how to be more emotionally intelligent (without trying so hard)

text: Hudson's image: joy is the {{c1::matriarch}} of a family of emotions. She will not come into your house if {{c2::her children}} are not welcome.
extra: The same idea as "joy arrives once the other feelings are let in".
source_title: 50 lessons on how to be more emotionally intelligent (without trying so hard)

front: Hudson: how can you tell caretaking from love?
back: Caretaking has no buzz. He calls it a watered-down version of love.
source_title: 50 lessons on how to be more emotionally intelligent (without trying so hard)

front: What do a balloon and a guitar string show about relationships, in Hudson's view?
back: Some tension is needed for life. Without it a balloon goes flat and a string loses its tune. A relationship is the same.
source_title: 50 lessons on how to be more emotionally intelligent (without trying so hard)

front: Why does Hudson call meditation alone an inefficient tool for self-discovery?
back: It is like building a house with only a saw. It can be done, but it takes a very long time.
source_title: 50 lessons on how to be more emotionally intelligent (without trying so hard)

front: Try now, 30 seconds: how could you become 10% more connected, to yourself or the person with you?
back: Notice that you can answer at once, for example eye contact or feeling your body. Hudson says everyone has this access at any time.
extra: He asks this instead of answering "how do I get more connected?". If connecting with others feels hard, connect 10% more with yourself.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson: when you feel unsettled before a decision, where do you put your attention to calm down?
back: Outward, on your senses: what you see and hear, from the skin out. Going inward can unsettle you more.
extra: His image: a veteran hears a car backfire in Ohio and is back in Fallujah. The senses bring you to the present. The inner experience may still be in the past.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson: what is the difference between a choice and a decision?
back: A choice just happens, with no deliberation. If you are deliberating over a decision, you are already in fear.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson's thought experiment: what if you were sure that being homeless would be the happiest time of your life?
back: Then homelessness would not scare you. What you fear is the emotional experience you project into the future, not the event.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson's story from his 20s: what did he do when he started to feel abandoned, and what happened?
back: He got either hard ("fine then") or needy. Both made people leave, so he created the abandonment he tried to avoid.
extra: This is the Golden Algorithm in his own life.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson: how is a principle different from a value?
back: You can act on a principle. A value, such as "be honest", rarely helps you choose a car, an advisor, or whether to fire someone.
extra: He applies a principle all the way down. With "connection": how do I connect with my audience in marketing, with an unhappy employee, at the start of a meeting?
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Interviewer Andrew Horn's exercise: how can you find your own principles without theory?
back: Recall a time you were at your peak. See which principles you were living then. In your worst moments, they were often held back.
extra: This is the interviewer's exercise. Hudson tried it and said it fit: he was connected, embracing intensity, and treating everything as an iteration.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

text: Hudson's steps to welcome an emotion: 1. {{c1::See that it cannot oppress you}}. 2. {{c2::Get deeply curious about it in the body}}. 3. {{c3::Play experiments with it and see how it reacts}}. 4. {{c4::Its wisdom then shows itself}}.
extra: Jumping straight to loving every emotion usually fails. For step 1 with anger, he suggests dominating it once, alone. Never aim anger at a person without their consent.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: What does Hudson's bathroom comparison say about the discomfort of an emotion?
back: Needing the bathroom is not painful; holding it in is. Most of an emotion's discomfort is the resistance to it.
extra: He found this by experiment: tell the emotion to go away, sing show tunes to it, distract it, hug it. It changes when you meet it with welcome.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Two extra Emotional Inquiry questions Hudson likes: what are they?
back: Where does the sensation end and you begin? What is it like to step into its centre and look out?
extra: Also: how does the movement at the centre differ from the movement at the edge? He says these give space and closer contact at once.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Try with a partner, 5 minutes: put a problem you wrestle with as a "how" or "what" question. Then trade only how/what questions back.
back: Do not answer. Notice the blank, open feeling when your mind has no reply. Hudson calls this wonder, and says fear cannot exist in it.
extra: Closed yes/no questions do not work. Example from the talk: "How could a third child make me more free?"
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson: why does wonder help with a problem?
back: Most problems are context problems: you believe a set of assumptions. Wonder lets you question them.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson: what is "dirty fuel" for success?
back: Success driven by stress or a sense of not being enough, without self-understanding. It needs more fuel and never satisfies.
extra: He says the question is not whether you can succeed without inner work (you can). It is whether you can have the life you want.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson could retire. What does he say drives him to keep working long days?
back: "I'm just playing with Legos": he follows his enjoyment, as a child builds for fun, not because it is never enough.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: What idea from Hand in Hand Parenting taught Hudson to love his own emotions?
back: A young child who feels disconnected needs a big emotional experience to reconnect. He sat with his children in loving attention through it.
extra: He calls this way of parenting the most profound spiritual practice he has had.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson's Whole Foods story: what happened when his daughter screamed for chips he would not buy?
back: He sat on the floor and said he understood. When a woman asked if she was okay, his daughter said she was just having her emotions.
extra: It lasted about seven minutes. He says he knew then that he had learned to stay present with a big emotion.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson: how are we built to make big decisions?
back: In groups, not alone. A community of practice lets others reflect your decisions back to you.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson: why is holding back emotions a cause of stress?
back: To stop feeling, you must tighten your muscles. That held tightness is tension.
extra: He names two other causes: harsh self-talk, and a lack of connection with people.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson: what happens when stressed people treat others as a threat for long enough?
back: The others start to act like a threat. He sees this in politics, marriages and parenting.
source_title: The Art of Making Great Decisions w Joe Hudson (Full episode) - What's the Big Idea 54

front: Hudson's friend who kept overeating: what did he do instead of telling himself to eat less?
back: Each time he overate, he sat still for 10 minutes and felt the bloating. Over time he stopped overeating.
extra: Hudson's point: feel the pain of a habit fully, as with a hot frying pan, and you let go without willpower.
source_title: How To Be Disciplined Without Having Discipline (3 Tips)

front: Hudson: how do you avoid decision fatigue with a habit you want to cut?
back: Set up your life so there is no choice to make. Example: give the game controller to someone else, or hide it far away.
extra: Each time you see the temptation, you make a decision. Sooner or later you say yes, then beat yourself up.
source_title: How To Be Disciplined Without Having Discipline (3 Tips)

front: Hudson's replacement tip: what is the first step to replacing a habit?
back: Look honestly at what the habit gives you, such as a break, energy or forgetting your problems.
source_title: How To Be Disciplined Without Having Discipline (3 Tips)

front: Hudson's replacement tip: what must the substitute be, so it needs no discipline?
back: Something you enjoy that gives you the same thing in a healthier way. Example: riding horses or pickleball in place of video games.
source_title: How To Be Disciplined Without Having Discipline (3 Tips)

front: Hudson: when do you feel stuck?
back: When you see a few ways to get what you want and dislike the possible consequences of all of them. Stuck is a feeling, not a fact.
source_title: The More Stuck You Feel, The Closer You Are To Freedom

front: Hudson: how does fear shrink your options when you feel stuck?
back: It makes you see each option as one fixed way. "Ask for a promotion" can be said many ways, such as asking what it would take.
source_title: The More Stuck You Feel, The Closer You Are To Freedom

front: Hudson: when you hold back from a change, what do you think you trade, and what do you really trade?
back: You think you trade safety for risk. You really trade the known for an adventure.
source_title: The More Stuck You Feel, The Closer You Are To Freedom

front: Hudson's story of a vice president afraid to start a company: what did his questions show her?
back: If she failed, she would be more hirable. Her VP role likely lasted only a few years anyway, so staying was the bigger risk.
source_title: The More Stuck You Feel, The Closer You Are To Freedom

text: Hudson: what you call safety is often {{c1::stagnation}}, and what you call risk is often {{c2::iteration}}.
extra: He says the brain is built to avoid failing at the same thing again. So if you see a step as a possible failure, you resist it. If you see it as an iteration, it is just practice.
source_title: The More Stuck You Feel, The Closer You Are To Freedom

front: Hudson: does being yourself mean giving in to every impulse, like games or drinking all day?
back: No. You dislike those habits, and that shows they are not you. Who you want to be points to what you are.
source_title: Be Yourself and Watch Your Life Rearrange

front: Try now, 1 minute: ask "What have I always been? What has not changed about me?" Live in the question; do not look for an answer.
back: Notice a quieting. Hudson says the inner fight eases when you touch what you essentially are.
source_title: Be Yourself and Watch Your Life Rearrange

front: Hudson: what body signal shows you are not being yourself?
back: A strong constriction after an action, an "ugh, I shouldn't be doing this". Fear or anger can still be there when you are yourself.
extra: Another sign: a constant fight with yourself. If you fight yourself, which one is you?
source_title: Be Yourself and Watch Your Life Rearrange

front: Hudson: if you are not yourself, whom do your friends and your job suit?
back: The person you pretend to be. That causes friction everywhere. Being yourself builds a life that fits you, though some people may leave.
source_title: Be Yourself and Watch Your Life Rearrange

front: Hudson: how does being yourself change how much you care what others think?
back: The more you act from what is true for you, the less others' opinions matter. The less you are yourself, the more they matter.
extra: His story: a businessman turned politician used to make unpopular calls with ease. Once he held back his truth in politics, he began to care far more what people thought.
source_title: Be Yourself and Watch Your Life Rearrange

front: Hudson's story of a woman unsure about her job who started to speak her truth there: what happened?
back: The job changed to support who she is. He says this happens about 80% of the time; sometimes people quit or are fired.
extra: She used vulnerability from his course: say what is true even when it is a little scary.
source_title: Be Yourself and Watch Your Life Rearrange

front: Hudson: why do so many people chase love like hungry ghosts?
back: They are not being themselves. Love for a pretend self never feeds you, because someone else is being loved.
source_title: Be Yourself and Watch Your Life Rearrange

front: Hudson: what is the feeling of having no time usually about?
back: Emotional overwhelm and not being present, more than the real amount of time.
extra: Example: overwhelmed at night, you scroll to avoid it, sleep late, then rush again in the morning.
source_title: Your Emotions Control Your Time (Why We Always Feel So Busy)

front: Hudson and his co-host: how does the urgency of a fast pickleball rally differ from time scarcity?
back: In the rally you are present and outside time. Time scarcity puts you in the future, thinking about the next task.
extra: So feeling time-starved can be a sign that you are not present with what is going on in you.
source_title: Your Emotions Control Your Time (Why We Always Feel So Busy)

front: Hudson and his co-host: what is "emotional debt"?
back: Avoided feeling that grows. The more you avoid it, the more you need to avoid, so it compounds like a credit card.
extra: Paying it off can take less than you think, sometimes just a short cry.
source_title: Your Emotions Control Your Time (Why We Always Feel So Busy)

front: Hudson: which feeling drives looking-ahead time pressure, and which drives looking-back time pressure?
back: Ahead ("I don't have enough time") is mostly fear. Back ("I didn't have enough time for my kids") is mostly grief.
extra: Move the fear and the grief, and your attention can come back to now.
source_title: Your Emotions Control Your Time (Why We Always Feel So Busy)

front: Hudson: what question lets time work for you instead of you working for time?
back: What can I do today that will save me a lot of time next month? Plant a seed instead of foraging all day.
extra: Examples: up-front work with a child or a dog, or time spent connecting with someone.
source_title: Your Emotions Control Your Time (Why We Always Feel So Busy)

front: Hudson: why does he not book back-to-back meetings?
back: Each activity needs a period of rest and integration after it. Without it, loops stay open and meeting actions do not get done.
extra: One person he works with ends each meeting with five minutes in which everyone takes the first actions.
source_title: Your Emotions Control Your Time (Why We Always Feel So Busy)

front: Hudson's five minutes every two hours: what does he say to "I don't have time"?
back: It is about 40 minutes a day. If you lack that, you lack time for 40 minutes of social media too. Try it for one day.
source_title: Your Emotions Control Your Time (Why We Always Feel So Busy)

front: His co-host Brett Kistler: what may you notice in your first five minutes of doing nothing?
back: You rush through them, thinking of what comes next, to tick the box. That same stance creates your time scarcity.
extra: In those five minutes you could also cry, scream, feel fear, or just enjoy yourself.
source_title: Your Emotions Control Your Time (Why We Always Feel So Busy)

front: Hudson's story of the executives who adopted five-star meetings: what did one of them say soon after?
back: That they had no time for a new effort, minutes after saying they saved about 7 hours a week. The sense of no time stayed.
source_title: Your Emotions Control Your Time (Why We Always Feel So Busy)

front: How does Hudson say he rests, and what does he notice after?
back: He takes August off and short silent retreats each quarter. After them he feels he has plenty of time, and it is hard to rush.
extra: As of 2025. The further he gets from a break, the more the urgency returns.
source_title: Your Emotions Control Your Time (Why We Always Feel So Busy)
